subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What does the term 'population density' measure?
options: The total number of people living in a country
The average number of people living per square kilometre
The rate at which a population is growing each year
The number of births minus deaths per 1000 people
questions.explain: Population density is calculated as the total population divided by the land area, giving people per square kilometre.

questions.q: Which phrase best describes a sparsely populated area?
options: An area with many people relative to its size
An area with few people relative to its size
An area where the birth rate exceeds the death rate
An area experiencing high levels of immigration
questions.explain: Sparsely populated areas have a low population density, meaning relatively few people live there.

questions.q: Which physical factor would most likely discourage dense settlement in an area?
options: Flat, fertile lowland with good soils
A reliable supply of fresh water
Steep, mountainous relief with a harsh climate
A temperate climate with moderate rainfall
questions.explain: Steep relief and a harsh climate make farming, building and access difficult, so few people settle there.

questions.q: How is the birth rate defined?
options: The number of live births per 1000 people per year
The number of children born to one woman
The percentage increase in population each year
The number of live births per 100 people per year
questions.explain: Birth rate is the number of live births per 1000 people in a population in one year.

questions.q: How is the death rate defined?
options: The number of deaths per 100 people per year
The average age at which people die
The number of deaths per 1000 people per year
The percentage of a population over the age of 65
questions.explain: Death rate is the number of deaths per 1000 people in a population in one year.

questions.q: Which formula correctly gives the natural increase of a population?
options: Death rate minus birth rate
Birth rate minus death rate
Immigration minus emigration
Birth rate plus death rate
questions.explain: Natural increase is found by subtracting the death rate from the birth rate, and does not include migration.

questions.q: A country has a birth rate of 28 per 1000 and a death rate of 9 per 1000. What is its natural increase?
questions.explain: Natural increase = birth rate (28) minus death rate (9), which equals 19 per 1000.

questions.q: How many stages are shown in the demographic transition model used in the specification?
options: Three
Four
Five
Six
questions.explain: The demographic transition model has five stages, from high fluctuating to natural decline.

questions.q: What are the birth rate and death rate like in Stage 1 (high fluctuating) of the demographic transition model?
options: Both high
Both low
Birth rate low, death rate high
Birth rate high, death rate falling
questions.explain: In Stage 1 both birth and death rates are high, so the total population stays low and fairly stable.

questions.q: What mainly causes the rapid population growth seen in Stage 2 of the demographic transition model?
options: A rapid fall in the death rate while the birth rate stays high
A rapid rise in the birth rate while the death rate stays high
Both birth and death rates falling together
A death rate that is higher than the birth rate
questions.explain: Improved food, sanitation and medicine cut the death rate while the birth rate remains high, causing rapid growth.

questions.q: Which statement best describes Stage 4 (low fluctuating) of the demographic transition model?
options: High birth rate and high death rate
Low birth rate and low death rate
High birth rate and falling death rate
Death rate higher than birth rate
questions.explain: In Stage 4 both birth and death rates are low, so the population is high and stable.

questions.q: What happens to the population in Stage 5 of the demographic transition model?
options: It grows very rapidly
It stays high and stable
It falls because the death rate is higher than the birth rate
It stays low because both rates are high
questions.explain: In Stage 5 the birth rate drops below the death rate, causing a natural decrease in population.

questions.q: A country has a high birth rate, a rapidly falling death rate and very fast population growth. Which stage of the demographic transition model best fits it?
options: Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 4
Stage 5
questions.explain: A high birth rate with a rapidly falling death rate and fast growth is characteristic of Stage 2 (early expanding).

questions.q: Which definition best describes migration?
options: The movement of people from one place to another to live
The natural increase of a population over time
The number of births per 1000 people per year
The distribution of people across a country
questions.explain: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another, usually to live there for a period of time.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a push factor for migration?
options: Better job opportunities in a city
War and conflict in the home area
A warmer, more pleasant climate elsewhere
Higher wages in the destination country
questions.explain: Push factors are negative conditions, such as war, that drive people to leave their home area.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a pull factor for migration?
options: Drought and crop failure at home
Persecution in the home country
Better employment and higher wages in the destination
A shortage of housing in the home area
questions.explain: Pull factors are positive attractions of a destination, such as more jobs and higher wages.

questions.q: What does the term 'emigration' mean?
options: Moving into a country to live
Leaving a country to live in another
Moving from the countryside to a city
Being forced to flee across a border
questions.explain: Emigration is when a person leaves their country to settle in another country.

questions.q: What is the difference between a refugee and an economic migrant?
options: A refugee is forced to flee, while an economic migrant chooses to move for work
A refugee moves for a better job, while an economic migrant is forced to flee
Both are forced to leave their country against their will
There is no difference between the two terms
questions.explain: Refugees are forced to flee danger such as war or persecution, whereas economic migrants voluntarily move to seek work.

questions.q: In one year a country gains 5000 immigrants and loses 2000 emigrants. What is its net migration?
questions.explain: Net migration = immigration (5000) minus emigration (2000), giving a net gain of +3000.

questions.q: A rural area sees large numbers of young adults leaving to work in cities. Which impact is most likely on the area they leave?
options: An increasingly ageing population is left behind
A rapidly rising birth rate
Severe overcrowding and housing shortages
A large fall in the average age of the population
questions.explain: When young adults emigrate, the population left behind becomes older on average, leaving an ageing population.

specSource: CCEA GCSE Geography (2017) specification; Population & Migration
